text.p: A rally in oil prices was a main feature of fairly subdued commodity markets overnight

Oil prices rallied again with the help of news of a draw in U.S. stocks of refined oil products after surrendering on Tuesday some recent sharp gains. London October futures for North Sea benchmark Brent Blend crude oil at 1645 GMT were up by almost 40 cents a barrel at around $20.40. The NYMEX oil complex closed higher mostly on bullish inventory data, but gasoline led gains with the threat that Tropical Storm Fran will head toward the Hess refinery on St. Croix in the Carribean, traders said. October crude oil closed up 15 cents to $21.69 barrel, retreating from its intraday high of $22.10. A report that Iraq may be massing troops in northern Kurdish regions fueled crude's gains during the day, traders said.

Gold ended in London unchanged from Tuesday at $388.55 per ounce, while New York precious metals futures ended lower, slipping back after the monthly OTC options expiry. COMEX December gold ended down $1.00 an ounce at $393.00, after trading in a $394.10-392.90 range, with support around $393.00 now being tested, traders said. In New York bullion trade, spot gold was quoted at $387.90/388.40 from a New York close Tuesday at $388.80/389.20.

Copper was trapped in a band on the London Metal Exchange, barely reacting to news that workers at Chile state producer Codelco's Salvador mine voted to strike from Saturday to demand wage rises. Output at this mine is only a modest 85,000 tonnes a year. Last afternoon business was at $1,943 a tonne, down just $1 from Tuesday.

Aluminium activity was low-key, although the market's stability back above the $1,480 level was encouraging. The last trade was at $1,486.50, a $4.50 gain. Nickel business was confined to a narrow range as well, with prices edging towards the highs to close at $7,350, a $10 gain from Tuesday. Lead retained earlier gains above $800, which were notched up by Far Eastern buying and short-covering, closing at $805, a $10 advance. Zinc trade was slow, both in futures and in the physical sector, and last LME business was at $1,024, down just $1. Tin market conditions were equally slow, but prices held steady on the kerb, closing at an unchanged $6,175. Alloy was $7 higher at $1,285.

Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat futures closed lower on competition for U.S. export business amid increasing prospects for global wheat production, traders said. "There are bigger wheat crops coming in all over the world and that's weighing on wheat. No one wants it right now," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds. Pressure also came from good harvest weather for the U.S. spring wheat crop and prospects for heavy deliveries to be posted against the September Friday, first notice day for deliveries on the September contracts. Wheat closed 1-1/2 to 10-3/4 cents per bushel lower, with September down seven at $4.51-1/4.

London white sugar finished mostly weaker with buyers staying on the sidelines and activity centred on switches, traders said. The front-month October contract closed down $1.70 at $349.00 per tonne, just 30 cents above its session low. SCE world sugar futures ended little changed Wednesday, after trading in a narrow range, following gains Tuesday.
CSCE October sugar ended off just 0.01 cent at 11.73 cents, after trading in a 11.67-11.74 cents a lb range.
